original.title: Whose Science? Whose Knowledge?
original.note: Record dated 2016 (later printing of the 1991 book).

core_idea: Knowledge is shaped by the social position of those who produce it. Starting research from the lives of marginalized groups, such as women, can reveal aspects of social relations that are invisible from dominant positions. Harding argues this yields 'strong objectivity': more objective knowledge, because researchers examine their own social location instead of claiming a view from nowhere.
key_concepts_note: Use the concepts already stored for this theory in the library (theories.concepts).
when_to_use: How do women or other marginalized groups experience and understand an institution, a policy or a workplace?
Whose knowledge counts in a field, and what is missed when research starts from dominant groups?
Typical data: in-depth interviews, life histories, institutional ethnography, participatory methods.
common_mistakes: Claiming that being a woman automatically gives better knowledge. A standpoint is achieved through critical reflection, not given by identity.
Treating 'women' as one group without attention to race, class, ethnicity or location.
Using the term without addressing your own position as researcher.
